function.name: patch
function.description:
Targeted find-and-replace edits in files. Use this instead of sed/awk in terminal. Uses fuzzy matching (9 strategies) so minor whitespace/indentation differences won't break it. Returns a unified diff. Auto-runs syntax checks after editing.

REPLACE MODE (mode='replace', default): find a unique string and replace it. REQUIRED PARAMETERS: mode, path, old_string, new_string.
PATCH MODE (mode='patch'): apply V4A multi-file patches for bulk changes. REQUIRED PARAMETERS: mode, patch.

mode.description: Edit mode. 'replace' (default): requires path + old_string + new_string. 'patch': requires patch content only.

path.description: REQUIRED when mode='replace'. File path to edit.

old_string.description: REQUIRED when mode='replace'. Exact text to find and replace. Must be unique in the file unless replace_all=true. Include surrounding context lines to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: REQUIRED when mode='replace'. Replacement text. Pass empty string '' to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false)

patch.description:
REQUIRED when mode='patch'. V4A format patch content. Format:
*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: path/to/file
@@ context hint @@
 context line
-removed line
+added line
*** End Patch

function.name: process
function.description: Manage background processes started with terminal(background=true). Actions: 'list' (show all), 'poll' (check status + new output), 'log' (full output with pagination), 'wait' (block until done or timeout), 'kill' (terminate), 'write' (send raw stdin data without newline), 'submit' (send data + Enter, for answering prompts), 'close' (close stdin/send EOF).

action.description: Action to perform on background processes

session_id.description: Process session ID (from terminal background output). Required for all actions except 'list'.

data.description: Text to send to process stdin (for 'write' and 'submit' actions)

timeout.description: Max seconds to block for 'wait' action. Returns partial output on timeout.

offset.description: Line offset for 'log' action (default: last 200 lines)

limit.description: Max lines to return for 'log' action

function.name: read_file
function.description: Read a text file with line numbers and pagination. Use this instead of cat/head/tail in terminal. Output format: 'LINE_NUM|CONTENT'. Suggests similar filenames if not found. Use offset and limit for large files. Reads exceeding ~100K characters are rejected; use offset and limit to read specific sections of large files. NOTE: Cannot read images or binary files — use vision_analyze for images.

path.description: Path to the file to read (absolute, relative, or ~/path)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed, default: 1)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read (default: 500, max: 2000)

function.name: search_files
function.description:
Search file contents or find files by name. Use this instead of grep/rg/find/ls in terminal. Ripgrep-backed, faster than shell equivalents.

Content search (target='content'): Regex search inside files. Output modes: full matches with line numbers, file paths only, or match counts.

File search (target='files'): Find files by glob pattern (e.g., '*.py', '*config*'). Also use this instead of ls — results sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: Regex pattern for content search, or glob pattern (e.g., '*.py') for file search

target.description: 'content' searches inside file contents, 'files' searches for files by name

path.description: Directory or file to search in (default: current working directory)

file_glob.description: Filter files by pattern in grep mode (e.g., '*.py' to only search Python files)

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 50)

offset.description: Skip first N results for pagination (default: 0)

output_mode.description: Output format for grep mode: 'content' shows matching lines with line numbers, 'files_only' lists file paths, 'count' shows match counts per file

context.description: Number of context lines before and after each match (grep mode only)

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Two patterns:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers).
  (2) Long-running tasks with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working on other things and the system auto-notifies you when the task finishes. Great for test suites, builds, deployments, or anything that takes more than a minute.
For servers/watchers, do NOT use shell-level background wrappers (nohup/disown/setsid/trailing '&') in foreground mode. Use background=true so Hermes can track lifecycle and output.
After starting a server, verify readiness with a health check or log signal, then run tests in a separate terminal() call. Avoid blind sleep loops.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Two patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers). (2) Long-running tasks paired with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working and get notified when the task finishes. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified exactly once when the process finishes. **This is the right choice for almost every long-running task** — tests, builds, deployments, multi-item batch jobs, anything that takes over a minute and has a defined end. Use this and keep working on other things; the system notifies you on exit. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with watch_patterns — when both are set, watch_patterns is dropped.

watch_patterns.description: Strings to watch for in background process output. HARD RATE LIMIT: at most 1 notification per 15 seconds per process — matches arriving inside the cooldown are dropped. After 3 consecutive 15-second windows with dropped matches, watch_patterns is automatically disabled for that process and promoted to notify_on_complete behavior (one notification on exit, no more mid-process spam). USE ONLY for truly rare, one-shot mid-process signals on LONG-LIVED processes that will never exit on their own — e.g. ['Application startup complete'] on a server so you know when to hit its endpoint, or ['migration done'] on a daemon. DO NOT use for: (1) end-of-run markers like 'DONE'/'PASS' — use notify_on_complete instead; (2) error patterns like 'ERROR'/'Traceback' in loops or multi-item batch jobs — they fire on every iteration and you'll hit the strike limit fast; (3) anything you'd ever combine with notify_on_complete. When in doubt, choose notify_on_complete. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with notify_on_complete — set one, not both.

content.description: Complete content to write to the file

Chapter 1 — The Anniversary

93|

Three years after the extraction, the Moon colony had transformed itself from a survival outpost into a thriving community. The scars of those desperate days had faded, replaced by the routines and rituals of settled life. But beneath the surface of normalcy, something was stirring.

94|

The anniversary celebration was meant to be a triumph. Instead, it became the prologue to a nightmare.

95|

Three years had passed since the extraction. Three years since the last of the original survivors had been lifted off the lunar surface and the colony had officially begun its transformation from emergency shelter to permanent settlement. Sarah Chen stood at the observation window of the newly expanded habitat module, watching the Earth rise over the southern highlands, and tried to remember what it felt like to be afraid.

96|

* * *

The work required patience and precision — qualities that had been tested to their limits over the long months of the mission. Every movement mattered, every decision carried weight that could not be measured in ordinary terms. They had learned to live with the pressure, to channel it into focus rather than fear. It was the only way to survive in an environment where mistakes meant more than inconvenience — they meant extinction.

"We're getting closer," someone reported, their voice carrying a note of cautious optimism. "The numbers are starting to align. We're not there yet, but we can see the path forward."

The news was met with quiet nods. They had learned not to celebrate too early. In this world, hope was a fragile thing — necessary for survival, but dangerous when allowed to outrun reality.

The anniversary celebration was in full swing behind her. Music played through the habitat's speakers, a mix of old Earth classics and new compositions written by colonists who had discovered talents they never knew they had. The hydroponics bay had been cleared out for the occasion, tables laden with the first full harvest of vegetables grown entirely in lunar regolith. People laughed, danced, and talked about the future with an optimism that had been hard to come by in those first desperate months.

100|

"You're brooding again," a voice said from beside her. Dr. Marcus Webb, the colony's chief medical officer, leaned against the wall with a cup of synthetic coffee in his hand.

101|

"I'm reflecting," Sarah corrected. "There's a difference."

102|

Marcus smiled. "There is. Brooding is what you do when you don't want to celebrate. Reflecting is what you do when you're trying to figure out what went wrong so you can fix it before it happens again." He took a sip of his coffee. "So which is it?"

103|

Sarah didn't answer immediately. She watched as a group of children ran past, their laughter echoing through the corridor. They had been born on the Moon, most of them, and had never known a world where gravity pulled you down or where the sky was blue. This was their home. And it was her job to keep it safe.

104|

"I just can't shake the feeling that we're missing something," she said finally. "Three years of peace, and no one's asking the hard questions anymore. We almost died out there. All of us. And now it's like everyone's decided the danger is over."

105|

"The danger of extinction is over," Marcus said. "The danger of complacency — that's a different threat. But you can't force people to live in fear, Sarah. They need to believe the future is bright."

106|

* * *

107|

The first case appeared on the morning of the fourth day of celebrations. A technician named James Okonkwo woke up with a fever, chills, and a rash spreading across his arms. By noon, three more colonists reported the same symptoms. By evening, the infirmary had admitted nine patients, and Dr. Webb had sent an urgent message to the colony director's office.

108|

Sarah was in a planning meeting when the message arrived. She read it on her tablet, her face growing pale as she scanned the numbers. Nine cases in less than twelve hours. Unknown origin. Unknown transmission vector. Preliminary diagnostics indicated a pathogen unlike anything in the medical database.

109|

"We need to lock down the colony," she said, standing up so abruptly that her chair tipped over. "Right now."

110|

The other council members stared at her. Director Morrison, a career administrator who had been sent from Earth six months ago to oversee the colony's transition to self-governance, frowned. "That seems premature, Dr. Chen. We don't even know what we're dealing with yet."

111|

"That's exactly why we need to lock down," Sarah said. "If this is airborne —"

112|

* * *

The data painted a complex picture, layers of meaning stacked upon each other like geological strata. Each reading, each measurement, each observation contributed to an understanding that was slowly taking shape. But the process was painstaking, requiring them to question every assumption and verify every conclusion.

"We need to consider all possibilities," the lead scientist cautioned. "Even the ones that seem unlikely. The history of discovery is filled with breakthroughs that came from considering what others had dismissed."

The reminder was unnecessary but welcome. They knew the stakes. They knew what was riding on their work. And they knew that the only way forward was through rigorous, uncompromising honesty with the data and with themselves.

113|

"If this is airborne, locking us all in together is the worst thing we could do." Morrison's voice was calm, measured. "Let Dr. Webb do his work. We'll make decisions based on data, not speculation."

114|

Sarah wanted to argue, but she held her tongue. Morrison was technically correct. But she had learned something in those three years of survival: by the time you had enough data to be certain, it was often too late.

115|

* * *

116|

The colony's population had grown to nearly five hundred, spread across six interconnected habitat modules. Each module was a self-contained ecosystem — living quarters, workstations, recreation areas, and the ever-present hydroponics bays that provided fresh food and recycled air. Sarah moved through the corridors with the ease of someone who had walked them a thousand times, nodding to the people she passed, pausing occasionally to answer a question or offer a word of encouragement.

117|

In the three years since the extraction, the colony had undergone a remarkable transformation. What had begun as a desperate emergency shelter had become a thriving community. The original survivors had been joined by new arrivals from Earth — scientists, engineers, families who believed in the dream of a permanent human presence on the Moon. The infrastructure had expanded, the life support systems had been upgraded, and the agricultural output had tripled.

118|

But Sarah couldn't shake the feeling that it was all fragile. That beneath the surface of normalcy, something was waiting to go wrong. She had learned, in those terrible first months, that survival was not a destination but a continuous process. You never stopped fighting. You never stopped watching. You never stopped preparing for the worst.

119|

"You look like you're planning for a disaster," said a voice behind her. She turned to find Elena Vasquez, one of the new arrivals, carrying a tray of food from the celebration. "That's not very festive."

120|

Sarah forced a smile. "Old habits."

121|

"Habits can be unlearned. Come. Eat. Dance. Remember what it feels like to be alive." Elena handed her a plate. "The hydroponics team grew tomatoes for the first time. Real ones. You don't want to miss them."

122|

Sarah took the plate, its warmth seeping through her fingers. The first lunar-grown tomatoes. It was a milestone she had dreamed of during the dark days of the crisis. And now here they were. She looked at the celebration around her — the music, the laughter, the children running through the corridors — and allowed herself, just for a moment, to feel hope.

123|

* * *

124|

The investigation was proceeding slowly, each new piece of evidence raising more questions than it answered. Sarah moved through the colony like a ghost, her presence in corridors and meeting rooms becoming a familiar sight to the residents. She interviewed everyone who had come into contact with the soil samples, documented every timeline, cross-referenced every shift schedule. Patterns began to emerge — small inconsistencies that pointed toward a larger design.

125|

"The pathogen was engineered for stealth," Dr. Webb explained during one of their nightly briefings. "The incubation period, the symptoms, the progression rate — they were all calibrated to maximize spread before detection. Whoever designed this knew exactly what they were doing." He pulled up a chart on his tablet. "Look at the infection curve. It's textbook. Not a single deviation from the predicted model."

126|

* * *

The silence of the habitat was broken only by the steady hum of life support systems and the occasional crackle of the communication array. In the absence of external noise, the internal sounds of the human body became amplified — the beating of hearts, the rhythm of breath, the subtle movements that accompanied every thought and emotion.

"What are you thinking about?" someone asked, their voice soft in the dim light.

"About home. About the people we left behind. About whether they're thinking of us right now."

The question hung in the air, unanswerable. They were too far away for thoughts to travel, too isolated for connection. But they carried their memories with them, like talismans against the loneliness of space.

127|

Sarah studied the chart, her eyes tracing the exponential curve. "So we're dealing with professionals. Military-grade bioweapons experts."

128|

"Or corporate. These days, the line between the two is blurry."

129|

"Either way, they're operating on the Moon without authorization. That's a violation of every treaty and agreement signed since the original Space Treaty of 1967."

130|

"Treaties don't mean much when there's profit involved." Marcus leaned back in his chair. "The real question is: what do we do with this information? We can't exactly call the police. We are the police out here."

131|

Sarah had been thinking about that. The colony had no law enforcement beyond a small security team, no judicial system beyond the council's administrative authority. 158|

The idea was met with skepticism at first. But as they worked through the implications, a new understanding began to emerge. They had been asking the wrong questions. Now they knew what to ask. And the answers were waiting.

159|

Chapter 2 — Symptoms

By the end of the first week, the number of cases had risen to forty-seven. The infirmary was overflowing, and the colony's gymnasium had been converted into a makeshift treatment center. Dr. Webb and his team worked around the clock, but the pathogen defied every test they threw at it.

161|

The symptoms followed a pattern. First came the fever and chills, accompanied by a distinctive rash that started on the arms and spread inward toward the torso. Then came the neurological effects — confusion, memory lapses, difficulty concentrating. In the most severe cases, patients became disoriented to the point where they could no longer recognize their own family members.

162|

"It's like nothing I've ever seen," Marcus told the council during an emergency meeting called on the eighth day. He looked exhausted, dark circles under his eyes, his normally crisp medical coat rumpled and stained. "We've run every diagnostic we have. Sequenced the genome. It's not bacterial, not viral in any known classification. It's almost as if —" He stopped, struggling to find the words.

163|

"As if what?" Director Morrison demanded.

164|

"As if it were designed," Marcus said quietly.

165|

The room fell silent. Sarah watched the council members exchange glances. She could see the fear spreading through them, as infectious as the pathogen itself.

166|

"That's impossible," Morrison said, but his voice lacked conviction. "Who would design a disease? And why?"

167|

"I don't know," Marcus admitted. "But I do know that standard treatments are having no effect. Antibiotics don't work. Antivirals don't work. We're managing symptoms with supportive care, but unless we figure out what we're dealing with, people are going to start dying."

168|

Sarah raised her hand. "We need to consider the possibility that this wasn't an accident. That someone brought this into the colony intentionally."

169|

* * *

The work required patience and precision — qualities that had been tested to their limits over the long months of the mission. Every movement mattered, every decision carried weight that could not be measured in ordinary terms. They had learned to live with the pressure, to channel it into focus rather than fear. It was the only way to survive in an environment where mistakes meant more than inconvenience — they meant extinction.

"We're getting closer," someone reported, their voice carrying a note of cautious optimism. "The numbers are starting to align. We're not there yet, but we can see the path forward."

The news was met with quiet nods. They had learned not to celebrate too early. In this world, hope was a fragile thing — necessary for survival, but dangerous when allowed to outrun reality.

170|

"That's a serious accusation, Dr. Chen," Morrison said.

171|

"I'm not accusing anyone. I'm saying we can't afford to rule anything out." She turned to the council. "I want to form an investigative team. Review everything that came in on the last supply shipment. Every person who arrived in the last thirty days. Every piece of equipment that was brought into the habitat."

172|

"And who would lead this team?" Morrison asked.

173|

"I would."

174|

The council voted. The motion passed, but barely. Sarah Chen was now leading an investigation into a potential biological attack — a role she had never wanted and for which she had no training. But she was the only one asking questions, and that, she had learned, was the most important qualification of all.

175|

* * *

176|

In the infirmary, Dr. Marcus Webb was beginning to suspect that something was very wrong. The first patient — James Okonkwo — had presented with symptoms that looked like a standard viral infection. But the diagnostic tests had come back negative for every known pathogen in the colony's database. And his condition was deteriorating faster than Marcus had expected.

177|

"Run the panel again," he told his assistant, a young nurse named Priya Sharma. "Extended spectrum this time. Include everything in the library."

178|

"We already ran extended, doctor. Nothing."

179|

Marcus frowned. "Then run it again. And prepare a sample for genomic sequencing. I want to see what we're dealing with at the molecular level."

180|

He moved to James's bedside. The technician's skin was flushed, his breathing rapid and shallow. His eyes were open but unfocused, as if he were looking at something a million miles away.

181|

"James. Can you hear me?"

182|

James blinked slowly. "Doc?" His voice was a whisper. "What's happening to me?"

183|

* * *

The data painted a complex picture, layers of meaning stacked upon each other like geological strata. Each reading, each measurement, each observation contributed to an understanding that was slowly taking shape. But the process was painstaking, requiring them to question every assumption and verify every conclusion.

"We need to consider all possibilities," the lead scientist cautioned. "Even the ones that seem unlikely. The history of discovery is filled with breakthroughs that came from considering what others had dismissed."

The reminder was unnecessary but welcome. They knew the stakes. They knew what was riding on their work. And they knew that the only way forward was through rigorous, uncompromising honesty with the data and with themselves.

184|

"We're going to figure it out. Just rest. Let your body fight it."

185|

But as Marcus watched James's vital signs flicker on the monitor, he felt a cold certainty settling in his gut. This was not a natural infection. He had treated dozens of diseases, seen hundreds of cases, and nothing had ever looked quite like this. The pattern was wrong. The progression was wrong. Everything about it was wrong.

186|

And wrong, in Marcus's experience, usually meant dangerous.

187|

* * *

188|

The investigation was proceeding slowly, each new piece of evidence raising more questions than it answered. Sarah moved through the colony like a ghost, her presence in corridors and meeting rooms becoming a familiar sight to the residents. She interviewed everyone who had come into contact with the soil samples, documented every timeline, cross-referenced every shift schedule. Patterns began to emerge — small inconsistencies that pointed toward a larger design.

189|

"The pathogen was engineered for stealth," Dr. Webb explained during one of their nightly briefings. "The incubation period, the symptoms, the progression rate — they were all calibrated to maximize spread before detection. Whoever designed this knew exactly what they were doing." He pulled up a chart on his tablet. "Look at the infection curve. It's textbook. Not a single deviation from the predicted model."

190|

Sarah studied the chart, her eyes tracing the exponential curve. "So we're dealing with professionals. Military-grade bioweapons experts."

191|

"Or corporate. These days, the line between the two is blurry."

192|

"Either way, they're operating on the Moon without authorization. That's a violation of every treaty and agreement signed since the original Space Treaty of 1967."

193|

"Treaties don't mean much when there's profit involved." Marcus leaned back in his chair. "The real question is: what do we do with this information? We can't exactly call the police. We are the police out here."

194|

Sarah had been thinking about that. The colony had no law enforcement beyond a small security team, no judicial system beyond the council's administrative authority. If they were going to uncover the truth and hold the perpetrators accountable, they would have to build the infrastructure as they went.

Chapter 1 — The Landing Gone Wrong

331| 332|

The descent module Artemis-VII punched through the lunar sky at three thousand meters per second, its heat shield glowing cherry-red against the black. Inside, Dr. Elena Marchetti gripped her harness as the vibration rattled her teeth and the G-forces pressed her deeper into the acceleration couch. Beside her, Commander Jim Hawkes worked the manual override panel with the calm precision of a man who had trained for this exact moment ten thousand times in simulation.

333| 334|

"Twenty kilometers," Hawkes said, his voice flat through the intercom. "Deceleration nominal. Altitude markers matching."

335| 336|

Elena tried to swallow, but her throat was sandpaper. Six months of training in the Arizona desert, three weeks in orbit, and now this final plunge. She was a geologist, not a pilot. Her job was rocks, not rocketry. But the mission had been clear from the start: a six-person geological survey team, forty-five days on the lunar surface, core sampling from the South Pole-Aitken Basin. The most ambitious civilian science expedition ever mounted.

337| 338|

"Ten kilometers," Hawkes continued. "I'm seeing some fluctuation in the braking thrusters. Probably just telemetry lag."

339| 340|

Elena turned her head — a slow, heavy motion under the deceleration — and saw the indicator lights on the auxiliary panel. Two of them were blinking amber. That wasn't in the simulation manual.

341| 342|

"Jim," she said, "check your thruster balance on panel four."

343| 344|

A pause. Eight seconds of silence that felt like hours.

345| 346|

"I see it." Hawkes's voice had lost its flatness. Now it carried an edge Elena had never heard from him before. "We've got asymmetric burn. Starboard thrusters are underperforming by twelve percent."

347| 348|

Twelve percent. Elena's mind raced through the contingency training. Asymmetric burn meant the descent trajectory would drift. The automated guidance would try to compensate, but the margins on a lunar landing were razor-thin. There was no atmosphere to slow them, no parachutes, no backup systems beyond what was bolted to the hull.

349| 350|

"Can we correct?" she asked.

351| 352|

"Already trying. Switching to manual guidance mode." Hawkes's hands moved across the console, entering override codes. "Elena, I need you to call out altitude and vertical velocity from the secondary display. My panel's prioritizing attitude control."

353| 354|

Elena unclenched her fingers from the armrest and forced them toward the secondary screen. The numbers swam for a moment before resolving: altitude 4,200 meters, vertical velocity 62 meters per second, horizontal drift 180 meters and increasing.

355| 356|

"Four thousand meters, velocity sixty-two, drift one-eighty and climbing."

357| 358|

"Copy. Engaging correction burn."

359| 360|

The module shuddered as the port-side thrusters fired harder, trying to compensate for their lazy starboard counterparts. Elena felt the shift in vector, a sideways push that pressed her against the left side of her harness. The drift reading flickered: 175 meters. 170. 162.

361| 362|

"It's working," she breathed.

363| 364|

"Don't celebrate yet. Three thousand meters."

365| 366|

The ground was visible now through the forward viewport — not the smooth, gray plain she had expected, but a jumble of crater rims and ridges, sharp shadows cutting across the surface at oblique angles. They were coming in hot, and the terrain below was anything but flat.

367| 368|

"Two thousand meters. Drift stabilizing at forty meters. Thrusters at eighty-five percent."

369| 370|

A warning chime cut through the cabin. Elena's eyes snapped to the diagnostic panel. "Jim, the starboard thruster temperature is spiking. It's overheating."

371| 372|

"I see it. Shutting it down before it blows."

373| 374|

"If you shut it down, we lose half our braking—"

375| 376|

"I know."

377| 378|

The starboard thruster cut out with a clunk that Elena felt through the deck plates. The module immediately began to yaw, the horizon spinning past the viewport in a nauseating blur. Hawkes fought the controls, compensating with the remaining thrusters, but the descent had become a controlled fall rather than a landing.

379| 380|

"Five hundred meters. Velocity still forty-five. We're going to hit hard."

381| 382|

Elena braced herself, pressing her spine into the couch. The ground rushed up — a gray wall of rock and shadow — and then the remaining thrusters fired in a last desperate burn, kicking up a cloud of regolith that blotted out everything.

383| 384|

The impact was not a crash. It was worse: a grinding, tearing, skidding collision that threw Elena forward against her harness and filled the cabin with the screech of metal on stone. The module tipped, slid, and came to rest at an angle that left her hanging sideways, her vision swimming with stars and dust.

385| 386|

Silence. Then the hiss of escaping atmosphere.

387| 388|

"Jim?" Elena's voice was a rasp. "Jim, are you there?"

389| 390|

A groan from the command seat. "I'm here. I think my arm is broken. And we've got a hull breach."

391| 392|

Elena forced her eyes open and saw the red warning lights painting the cabin like a crime scene. They were down. They were alive. But the module was crippled, and somewhere in the chain of systems that had been designed to keep them alive for forty-five days, a dozen things were now broken.

393| 394|

The mission had become something else entirely.

395| 396|

It had become a fight for survival.

397|

* * *

398|

Time was running out. Sarah checked the chronometer for the hundredth time, watching the numbers tick down with grim certainty. They had lost so much already — colleagues, equipment, hope. But she refused to let them lose everything. The colony had been her dream, her life's work. She would not let it die in the cold darkness of the lunar night.

399|

"We can do this," she said, more to herself than to the others. "We have to do this."

400|

The others nodded, their faces set with determination. They had come too far to give up now. The final push was ahead of them, and they would face it together, as they had faced everything else. The Moon was unforgiving. But so were they.

401|

* * *

402|

The work continued through the long hours, each member of the team pushing themselves beyond the limits of exhaustion. They knew that the window of opportunity was narrow — that every moment of delay could mean the difference between success and failure. The stakes were simply too high to allow for hesitation or doubt.

403|

"We're making progress," someone reported, their voice weary but determined. "Slowly. But it's happening."

404|

The news was met with a mixture of relief and renewed determination. They had been working toward this moment for so long that the prospect of success seemed almost unreal. But here it was — tangible, measurable, within reach.

405|

"Keep going," came the reply. "We're almost there."

Her hands moved through the emergency shutdown sequence: main power off, auxiliary batteries online, cabin pressure isolation valves closed. The hissing stopped. 444| 445|

A thump from the aft hatch cut him off. Three short knocks. The emergency signal. Elena scrambled across the angled deck and pressed her helmet against the hatch, activating the external microphone.

446| 447|

"Identify yourself."

448| 449|

The monitors flickered with streams of data, each line representing a different variable in the complex equation of survival. Temperature, pressure, radiation, oxygen levels — the numbers danced across the screens in an endless ballet of information. But no machine could measure the most important variable: the human will to endure.

"We've faced worse," someone said, their voice steady with conviction. "We've been pushed to the edge before. And we've always found a way back."

The words were meant to comfort, but they carried the weight of truth. This was not their first crisis. It would not be their last. And each time, they had found within themselves reserves of strength they hadn't known existed.

455| 456|

"How long was he exposed?" Hawkes asked, already reaching for the oxygen mask.

457| 458|

"Maybe thirty seconds before I got him sealed," Yuki said. Her voice was steady, but her hands were shaking. "I had to drag him through the emergency hatch. The main corridor is—it's gone, Jim. The whole aft section is open to the surface."

They wrapped him in thermal blankets and secured him to the deck with cargo straps to prevent him from drifting in the low gravity.

461| 462|

"That's four of us," Elena counted. "Where are Dr. Mensah and Dr. Okafor?"

463| 464|

Yuki's face went tight. "I don't know. They were in the science module when the breach happened. The hatch sealed automatically, and I couldn't get it open again."

465|

The meeting stretched into its fourth hour, the arguments circling back to the same unresolved questions. They were trapped in a loop of analysis, unable to break free into decisive action. The problem was not a lack of information — it was an excess of it. Every new data point seemed to contradict the previous one, creating a maze of possibilities that led nowhere.

"Sometimes," the oldest member of the team said slowly, "the answer is simpler than we think. We've been looking for complex solutions because the situation seems overwhelming. But maybe we're missing the obvious because we're trying too hard."

The room fell silent. It was an uncomfortable thought — that the solution had been in front of them all along, hidden in plain sight by their own sophistication.

466| 467|

Hawkes struggled to his feet, cradling his broken arm. "The science module is connected through the main tunnel. If that's also breached—"

468| 469|

"Then they're either dead or trapped," Yuki finished. "We have to assume they followed emergency protocols. If they had time to suit up, they'll be waiting for rescue."

470| 471|

"And if they didn't?" Elena asked.

472| 473|

No one answered. The silence stretched, filled only by the beep of monitors and the thin whistle of air circulating through the battery-powered scrubbers.

474| 475|

"We need to establish a baseline," Hawkes said finally. "Full inventory of supplies, oxygen, water, food. We need to know exactly how long we can survive with what we've got. Then we figure out how to get a signal out to Earth."

476|

* * *

Every movement mattered, every decision carried weight that could not be measured in ordinary terms. They had learned to live with the pressure, to channel it into focus rather than fear. 479| 480|

"I'll take inventory," she said. "Yuki, check the comms system. If the main antenna is damaged, we might be able to jury-rig something from the spare parts."

481| 482|

"And if the spare parts are in the aft section?" Yuki asked.

483| 484|

"Then we get creative."
